# Copper October 2011 

- Having lost a quarter of its value during September it would have been easy to expect that the bloodletting was over and prices would at least stabilise during October.  Indeed, as meetings and negotiations at LME week underscored the fact that the world hadn’t as yet ended and that it probably wouldn’t next year either, cash quotes continued to bounce around.  But it was not until European leaders finally brokered a deal that they hope will draw a line under the regional debt crisis that the red metal was able to decisively recover some lost ground. 

- Despite the dramatic decline in prices in recent months we have not fundamentally altered our market outlook.  Given this price correction, the traditional price/stocks relationship which was stretched previously, is now less so.  And, while we have toned down both consumption and production forecasts by a percentage point or two, this has not had a significant effect on our supply/demand balance for the year, although there is a major change to our fourth quarter price forecast.  This is ultimately a reflection of the market’s ongoing cautious view of the outlook for demand, exacerbated by waves of renewed global debt concerns; these were also responsible for initially triggering the flight of capital across the LME complex, despite the fact that metal stocks remain well below comfortable levels.  We now forecast that prices will average $7700/t in the fourth quarter which puts the 2011 full year average price at $8868/t. 

- Any hopes for an Indian summer have turned to a chill, with demand conditions generally soft in Europe and North America, while activity in China is also easing.  While debt continues to dominate the headlines, this has yet to feed through into hard economic data, although it is fair to say that semis producers tend to report a cautious tone from their customers and as such, in their own purchases of cathode.  Demand, however, certainly has not ground to a halt. 

- Progress in the annual Mating Season negotiations has been rather slow over the past month.  With many buyers and sellers now well into their first round discussions we have yet to hear of numbers being tabled by any of the parties involved.

## Market Developments 

**Bloodletting slows in October** Having lost a quarter of its value during September it would have been easy to expect that the bloodletting was over and prices would at least stabilise during October.  Indeed, as meetings and negotiations at LME week underscored the fact that the world hadn’t as yet ended and that it probably wouldn’t next year either, cash quotes continued to bounce around.  But it was not until European leaders finally brokered a deal that they hope will draw a line under the regional debt crisis that the red metal was able to decisively recover some lost ground (however, time will tell whether this was just a knee-jerk reaction to some form of agreement having been reached in what has been, and remains a painfully slow and indecisive process). 

**Cash quotes hit new 2011 low** Prices did indeed continue their descent at the start of the month, sliding below the $7000/t level as the latest act of the European debt crisis unfolded, before dovish comments from the US Fed chairman snapped a five day losing streak and sent the red metal up to $7500/t.  Prices spent the next ten or so days stuck in a trading range between $7200/t and $7500/t, with investors sufficiently sceptical of European politicians’ ability to draw a line under the region’s debt troubles to push cash quotes any higher.  Copper decisively broke out of this pattern on the 19<sup>th</sup> , when it emerged that France and Germany were at odds over details of the latest euro bailout talks, sending copper down by almost 10% over a two day period to hit its low for the month, and indeed, the year, of $6721.50/t on 20<sup>th</sup> .  While concerns towards the euro zone debt crisis eased following their weekend summit, it was positive economic data from China that cheered the market and drove prices higher.  This was then followed by news that a deal had been reached to resolve the crisis and sent copper prices back above the $8000/t level. 

**Supply side fails to lift gloom** Despite the widespread gloom in the market place, prices ought to have been reasonably well supported by supply side issues that surely would otherwise have seen cash quotes move higher.  In particular, the ongoing strike at Freeport’s Grasberg operations would appear to be no closer to resolution, and despite the mine being able to operate at around 50-60% of capacity, on and off, using skeleton staff, the company had to declare force majeure on concentrate shipments towards the end of last month.  A strike is also ongoing at Cerro Verde in Peru, although production rates are being maintained through the use of staff, returning strikers and contract workers. It would appear that these strikes are having more of an impact on TC/RCs and on Mating Season negotiations than on the copper price and we discuss this in more detail in the concentrates section. 

**Annual LME gathering reveals miners’ confi

dence** The main themes emanating from this year’s LME week gathering seem to be that miners are relatively unconcerned by short-term price volatility stemming from the European debt crisis as prices are still well above average and indeed marginal costs of production. The same cannot be said for the financial community who are much more exposed to wild swings in prices and as such, feel more than a little bruised and battered by the collapse in most commodity prices over the past couple of months. A major double-dip recession and the attendant decline in demand would certainly be of concern to all parties, although this is not what we forecast as a base case. Indeed, even if key western economies were to contract, the downturn in consumption would most likely be much shallower than the 15% decline in 2009, mainly because stocks through the consumption chain are much leaner now than was the case back then. It is also worth noting that this is, in part, due to high copper prices and tighter credit conditions making it difficult from a cash flow perspective for consumers to hold large inventories. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - October 2011 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **LME stocks move lower on Asian cancellations** After the rise in cancelled warrants in September, a decline in stocks at LME warehouses was to be expected in October and this duly came. Having ended the month at 475kt, metal inventories currently stand at c.435kt, with the vast majority of this decline coming from Asian locations, and South Korea in particular. Although trade data isn’t yet available to confirm this, the material is reportedly headed for China. At the time of writing, stocks in Singapore had actually increased in October, although a sharp increase in cancelled warrants suggests this trend will be reversed in November. Indeed, cancelled warrants across LME warehouses as a whole have continued the increase that began in September, pointing to a further decline in overall stocks in the coming month. In Shanghai, SHFE stocks also moved lower, ending the month at 74kt, down from 98kt at September’s close. In tandem with the broad declines across Asia, bonded warehouse stocks also declined in October, reversing the increase from the prior month and now stand at around 200kt down from c.400kt in September. The increase in bonded warehouse stocks last month was partly related to collateral requirements, but also a reflection of material

**Chinese imports enjoy first year-on-year gain since January…** The arbitrage window between LME and Shanghai prices was open for most of August and as a result, imports continued their recent impressive form in September’s data release. Metal receipts rose by 14.2% year on year to 275.5kt, marking the highest level thus far in 2011 and in fact, the highest level since May of 2010 as a number of factors combined to draw in material. Firstly, the open arbitrage window in August encouraged traders to ship material into China but there were other factors at play as well, not least the requirements of consumers. However, the arbitrage window slammed shut in September with Shanghai prices not totally mirroring the precipitous fall seen on the LME, but as we noted above, the decline in stocks and the increase in cancelled warrants at Asian warehouses suggest that imports into China will remain strong for the time being at least. **..supported by tight scrap, restocking and financing** Given that in three of the last four months the arbitrage window was closed (i.e. with SHFE trading at a discount to LME) on average suggests that material heading for China now is not being shipped for speculative purposes. The obvious conclusion therefore is that this material must be destined for more traditional use and as such, indicative of strong demand. However, we know that Chinese underlying demand is slowing and the increase in shipments into the country may simply be a reflection of a slowdown in domestic refined production given the current tightness in concentrate markets. It is also worth noting that the decline in copper prices has seen scrap availability dry up, exacerbated by port congestion, which has resulted in rising scrap prices with cathode either being favoured by semis producers or simply that they have no choice but to use refined material because of lack of scrap. Meanwhile, those mills with solid cash flows and reasonable visibility in their order books are also taking the opportunity to increase their stocks. An alternative explanation, however, is that traders are shipping material in order to take advantage of the strength in premia in China which we discuss below. **Chinese premia remain elevated** Chinese premia peaked this month at around $150/t but have since eased back to $115/t. Several factors are at play in keeping Chinese premia at these e

levated levels, some of which were mentioned above. Another less obvious factor is the healthy demand within China for metal for financing purposes. Companies that have used copper as collateral to obtain loans have seen the value of that metal decline and as such have had to increase their collateral and thus their holdings of copper. This has created additional “demand” helping to buoy premia up to these elevated levels. Meanwhile, European premia have edged higher to between $50 to 70/t as players cautiously return to the market following the summer shutdowns and LME week. **Q4 prices forecast slashed** Despite the dramatic decline in prices in recent months we have not fundamentally altered our market outlook. Given this price correction, the traditional price/stocks relationship which was stretched previously, is now less so. And, while we have toned down both consumption and production forecasts by a percentage point or two, this has not had a significant effect on our supply/demand balance for the year, although there is a major change to our fourth quarter price forecast. This is ultimately a reflection of the market’s ongoing cautious view of the outlook for demand, exacerbated by waves of renewed global debt concerns; these were also responsible for initially triggering the flight of capital across the LME complex, despite the fact that metal stocks remain well below comfortable levels. We now forecast that prices will average $7700/t in the fourth quarter which puts the 2011 full year average price at $8868/t. We also remain of the opinion that the market will remain fundamentally tight during 2012, with China being the main engine of consumption growth, with pent up demand reinvigorated by credit easing. While debt continues to dominate the headlines, this has yet to feed through into hard economic data, although it is fair to say that semis producers tend to report a cautious tone from their customers and as such, in their own purchases of cathode. Demand, however, certainly has not ground to a halt. ### **Europe and CIS** **Euro debt crisis rumbles on** It is difficult to know where to start even when attempting to merely summarise the latest economic backdrop given the increasingly long and winding nature of the European debt crisis but suffice to say, a full discussion is beyond the scope of this publication. It might even be beyond the scope of the library of Pergamum. The significance of the crisis is of course the effect on consumer confidence, which will ultimately hurt demand for copper without a resolution. At present though, this hasn’t translated through into economic activity, with eurozone IP showing solid improvement in August. At some point, however, economic activity will track lower to match dour consumer sentiment or sentiment will improve to match the not that bad economic data. **Consumer reticence tempers semis orders** Sluggish output and order levels at semis producers following the summer shutdowns have continued into October, with firms noting that the negative economic backdrop is weighing heavily on consumer sentiment. While stocks were already at low levels ahead of the latest act in the Greek debt tragedy, uncertainty over the outlook has resulted in end users paring back inventories even further. Some have then placed larger orders for the start of 2012, creating stock financing and operating headaches for mills as they have to manage lumpy order books. However, that is not to say no business is being done and there is clearly an improvement from the summer lull but the ongoing debt crisis that we mentioned above has added an extra layer of caution to proceedings. **Auto sector races ahead** On a sectoral basis, automotive remains the strongest area for end use demand, w

ith wire rod producers reporting sustained strong order books.  Within Europe as a whole the performance of the sector is quite mixed but it is the German market which continues to lead activity overall, which as we have noted previously, is helpful for copper demand because of the greater average metal intensity of German cars.  On a less positive note, however, the construction markets remain subdued, with prospects here looking worse rather than better amid renewed risks of a major banking crisis. 

**Renewables no longer leaving other sectors green with envy** In the aftermath of the end of Germany’s nuclear era there was a lot of talk on the bright outlook for renewable energy, while those with a keen interest in copper watched hopefully from the sidelines given the extensive use of copper in these projects.  However, against a backdrop of fiscal austerity, there has been a lack of clarity or progress on future plans for the delivery of new green energy projects. Those projects that are in place and in construction continue to support demand to an extent but the shortage of activity on new projects leaves the horizon somewhat cloudy. 

**Premia edge higher** As we noted above, there is a cautious tone to copper demand at the moment, although despite this premia have edged up from the prior month.  We noted in our previous publication that premia were partly low as a result of sluggish demand but also because of some gaming of demand conditions ahead of LME week negotiations. The increase in premia to the $50-70/t range reflects players returning to the market, albeit cautiously, following LME week. 

**FY demand to slip lower** Although our full year view of demand is broadly in line with last month, we have made some minor adjustments with the net effect that we now expect demand to contract in Western Europe this year.  We had always expected a sluggish year in 2012 and this has not altered but we have nudged up our growth forecast for 2013 on the view that there should at least be some signs of life returning to economic activity by then. 

### **Americas** 

**Macro economic data somewhat encouraging…** Advance estimates of US Q3 GDP growth came in at a seasonallyadjusted annualized rate of 2.5%, according to data from the Commerce Department.  This was in line with analyst expectations and a significant pick-up on the prior quarter’s 1.3% and just 0.9% for the first half.  Industrial production edged up by just 0.2% last month, jobless claims fell to 402k in the middle week of this month, and orders for durable goods rose by 1.7% in September.  The fact that GDP did rise in Q3 by an amount which keeps the US “treading water” was interpreted as positive by the market, which continues to fear a double-dip recession.  However, it remains insufficient to put a dent in the 9.0-9.1% unemployment rate, which continues to be the top concern of the Obama administration. 

**..but micro markets such as housing show little signs of a turn around**

However, data for the all-important housing market continue to show that there is little room for optimism.  While sales of new single-family homes rose by 5.7% in September from August levels, the seasonally adjusted annualized rate of just 313k new home sales suggests that this

could represent a record low since record-keeping began in the early 1960s.  Tube producer Mueller Industries reported a 44% decline in net income during the third quarter, to US$10.5M, and cited a subdued forthcoming quarter for the construction market even if there appear to be select areas of promise, such as multi-family home construction and commercial construction rates.  The company concurs with the general conclusion that the unemployment rate has to come down before there will be a wider improvement in relevant copper markets. 

**SDI-OmniSource receives approval for new rod line** Despite some ongoing local opposition, Steel Dynamics Inc and its subsidiary OmniSource has received approvals from Indiana’s environment regulators to establish its US$39M, 198kt/a capacity copper wire rod plant at New Haven.  An air quality permit was issued on October 11<sup>th</sup> , and will allow the plant to release up to 71.3kt/a of greenhouse gases plus particulates, although it is not known precisely what the anticipated levels of the emissions will be.  Receipt of the permit should keep the plant on track for a late-2012 start. 

**KPS expands copper interest with UCI acquisition** New York City-based KPS Capital Partners LP has expanded its reach into copper markets with the late-September acquisition of United Copper Industries of Denton, TX for an undisclosed sum.  UCI has a c.80kt/a capacity Properzi rod mill which it established in 1998.  Much of its rod is consumed in-house at Denton, being drawn down to commercial and residential building wire applications.  Prior to the acquisition by KPS, UCI was an affiliate of the Industrias Unidas SA Group of Mexico (IUSA), which owns a copper smelter, refinery and rod mill at Pasteje, Mexico and the Cambridge Lee Industries and Reading Tube operations in the USA.  For its part, KPS Capital Partners already owns Global Brass and Copper which it formed by acquiring Olin Brass, Olin Metals and Chase Brass in November 2007 for US$400M.  GBC makes copper and alloy sheet products, strip, plate, small diameter rod and foil, and makes use of the A.J. Oster company as distributor, which also came with that late-2007 acquisition.  Buying UCI’s plant brings KPS into a new market area, although one which has been running on tight margins since the collapse of the North American construction markets in late-2008.  KPS Capital Partners LP is the manager of the KPS Special Situations Funds which has US$2.9Bn committed to restructurings, turnarounds and other special situations. 

**IMC adds rod capacity** Not for the first time this year, we fin

d ourselves writing about yet more capacity additions to the US wire rod market – but this time it is in the niche area of electroplating.  IMC-Metals America LLC, based in Shelby, North Carolina, and owned by scrap collector-distributor, Prime Materials Recovery Inc., is now producing undisclosed amounts of oxygen-free copper rod in the 8.0mm, 12.5mm and 19mm dia range.  IMC has used its own vertical casting techniques dating back to the mid-1980s, and this latest equipment addition of a multi-strand conticaster is also its own technology, rather than the more familiar names of UpCast and Rautomead.  The company tells us its rod capacity depends on the order pattern and is far from being established, but it claims that it is sufficient to satisfy the available market as IMC knows it currently.  For the future, IMC has the means, space and infrastructure to install additional capacity as required.  IMC’s main markets are copper anodes for electroplating. 

### **China** 

**Bulls and bears battle over meaning of economic data** Economic data releases out of China gave comfort to both bulls and bears over the past month, with industrial output up but inflation and GDP both moving lower.  Industrial production growth picked up its pace again in September, expanding by 13.8% year on year, after slowing the previous month.  Meanwhile, inflation slowed again in the latest reading, edging down to 6.1% in September from 6.2% the prior month, although still at a relatively elevated level.  Copper bulls will be hoping that the slowdown in Q3 GDP is helping to pull down inflation, without overly dampening industrial output.  Our view is that this is indeed what is happening. 

**Chinese stocks not so full of shock** The widespread reporting of estimates of Chinese copper stocks by the CNIA have left many commentators scratching their heads at the absolute levels if not the direction of movement.  According to CNIA, total stocks in China, including SHFE warehouses, were 300kt at the end of 2008, 1314kt in 2009 and 1900kt by the end of 2010.  This compares to our own estimates of 398kt for 2008, 1245kt at the close of 2009 and 1496kt at the end of last year.  Just from eyeballing the numbers, the CNIA estimate for 2008 simply feels too low, representing only 21 stock days of consumption.  The increase in stocks between 2008 and 2009 implies that China soaked up the whole of the 2009 copper market’s global surplus, which doesn’t seem unreasonable to us given the collapse in ex-China global demand that year.  However, what does seem unreasonable is a further c.600kt increase in stocks in 2010 against the backdrop of a global market deficit.  It could conceivably be that through the whole supply chain there was an increase of this magnitude or even bigger but if that was the case it would be wrong to classify that as a stock build of refined copper as a build up of copper semis at an end user constitutes refined copper that has already been consumed.  A further

explanation could be that the Chinese are trying to game market sentiment in a bid to drive prices lower, which as a net importer does seem plausible, especially given the requirement to restock following the draw down of stocks so far this year that tight credit conditions have caused. 

**Golden week takes shine of copper demand** Copper consumption in October was dampened somewhat by the golden week holiday in early October and as a result output at most fabricators was softer than in September.  Amid a backdrop of highly volatile copper prices, uncertainties over the global economic outlook and softening order books, semis producers ought to be maintaining inventories at low levels but the current relative cheapness of copper has prompted some firms with solid cash flows to build up stock levels.  Despite the slowdown in activity in that we have described, we reiterate our forecast of Chinese refined demand growth of 8% this year.

With relatively narrow spreads as scrap supply dries up in response to softer copper prices, some fabricators are now favouring cathode over scrap, which is also supporting refined demand.  Some Chinese up casting wire rod mills fed by scrap have cut production or in extreme cases temporarily shut down, improving margins at some of the bigger wire rod mills employing the imported SCR or conti-rod production lines. 

**Imports regain heady heights** Imports of refined copper hit their highest level this year to maintain the recovery from the May nadir and in fact were at the highest absolute level since May of 2010.  Moreover, with LME stock levels across Asia sliding sharply lower, it would be reasonable to assume that the imports into China will maintain their recent strength.  Imports rose by 14.2% year on year to 275kt in September, marking their first positive growth on the year ago figure since January of this year. 

**Strength in premia down to financing** The strength in premia from September has continued through October although as with the prior month, much of this is down to financing rather than robust underlying demand.  Certainly, demand condition remain healthy, even if, as we noted above, exhibiting signs of slowdown but the marginal increase in premia is down to the need to post collateral by borrowers as copper prices have tumbled. 

**Upturn in power investment sparks sector into life** Investment in the power grid increased by 29% in September from a month earlier, marking a sharp upturn from relatively sluggish activity so far this year.  In the first 9 months, investment in power increased by 7.9%, while investment in power generating and the grid increased by 5.1% and 11.3%, respectively.  In line with this demand for wire rod for power cable turned higher in October. 

**Transport sector moves up the gears** Automotive production increased by 15% from a month earlier in September, underscoring t

he continued recovery of car output, although it must be noted that September should be considered as a traditionally strong month for the industry. Auto production in the first nine months of the year is now up by 2.75%. Although auto production in Japan has recovered strongly, production in Thailand has been affected by the recent floods, with some producers shutting down production in mid-October. As a result, demand for Chinese made auto parts was relatively sluggish over the past month despite an apparent uptrend in domestic production. **Demand stripping off a layer** Strip production in October was also relatively subdued, especially connector strip and lead frame strip. With production shutting down at some electronic plants in October in Thailand due to flooding, exports of Chinese electronic components were hit and the slowdown in exports of semiconductors and LEDs dragged demand for lead frame strip lower. Meanwhile, air conditioner production in October remained underwhelming, reflecting the slowing trend as we move into this sector’s low season. shrugs off slowdown concerns** While we have been concerned about the Japanese economic recovery running out of steam, industrial output data for August suggests that isn’t the case, for now at least.  Industrial production climbed yet again on a month-on-month basis, despite many workers taking holidays in the middle of the month, with the comparison on a year ago now down to minus 1%.  At the same time, the lumpy new machinery orders series continues to show improvement, pointing to further momentum to come from industrial output. 

**Slide in shipments a concern not a disaster** On the face of it the decline in shipments of wire and cable in September looks quite negative for the final part of the year, although things shouldn’t be looked at in quite such a negative light. Shipments fell by 1.6% year on year to 59.5kt, although this does mask strong growth from the prior month.  Certainly, shipments would be expected to increase on a month-on-month basis in any case as holidays typically dent output in August in Japan but significantly, September shipments were the highest level so far this year.  Weakness in shipments in the final quarter is in line with our forecast of a full year decline in demand but this still represents a relatively good outturn given what has gone before and what could have happened as a result. 

**Auto production back in the black** The recovery in Japanese automotive production continues apace, with output expanding positively on a year-on-year basis for the first time this year, despite a month-on-month fall.  Production of passenger cars climbed by 1.5% year on year in August, while the c.10% decline on the prior month should be confused for nothing more sinister than workers returning to their family homes in mid-August as is the tradition in Japan.  Car sales have also been improving and while not yet showing positive growth, they are at least building some momentum, which points to continued improvements in demand for copper semis from the sector. 

**Construction moves out of basement levels** The upturn in the Japanese construction market that we have been discussing over the last few months appears to have firmer foundations than previous “recoveries”.  As with automotive output, August data did reveal a negative month-on-month blip but the absolute level at over 80,000 units remains relatively strong, while year-on-year growth was impressive at 14%.  It would appear that at least some of this upturn is a result of reconstruction from the disaster of earlier in the year, which should sustain sectoral demand for copper well into 2012. 

**Concerns loom large for energy sector** Concerns over the outlook for energy producers cast a dark shadow over sectoral demand.  As firms cut back and reroute investment in the wake of the nuclear accident earlier this year, energy sector demand will be hit for at least the next year but possibly further out as well.

**Chinese concentrate imports remain at last year’s levels through October** Following the massive surge in August imports, Chinese concentrate receipts during September declined by 17.5% year on year

to 562.5kdmt.  On a cumulative basis this brings the 9-month total to 4.63Mdmt which is 6.6% lower than in the same period in 2010.  Chile, Australia and Peru remain the largest suppliers to this market, collectively accounting for 47% of the September total.  Mexico, Mongolia and the USA are also important contributors, adding a further 30% to the country’s imports.  On the basis of the numbers to date, China is likely to import around 6.1Mdmt in 2011 compared with 6.48Mdmt last year. 

**Sichuan Hongda aims to develop 200kt/a smelter project** Several Chinese smelter projects have come to the fore over the past month.  Sichuan Hongda Co. Ltd is looking to construct a 200kt/a copper smelter/refinery in the Shifang Industrial zone in Sichuan province as well as a 25kt/a ferromolybdenum plant and a 7.5kt/a molybdenum trioxide circuit. This would form the first stage of the project with future plans to double the capacity of the copper complex and to raise molybdenum output to 40kt/a at a later date.  The copper technology selected is based on flash smelting and refining as is currently used at the Xiangguang smelter in Shandong province.  The company’s finances have improved materially following a recent public listing.  In addition, Hongda has a close relationship with the regional government and there is a strong desire to promote industrial activity in the province in the wake of the devastating earthquake that hit the region in 2008.  Because of this, it is likely that this project will receive preferential treatment under the ‘post earthquake construction programme for promoting the local economy’.  That said, Hongda still needs environmental approval protection approval from the government before construction can commence at the project.  However, a positive outcome may be forthcoming as early as Q1 2012 which could see stage one in production by 2015.  The company is also developing a new copper-molybdenum mine in Tibet which would provide some of the feed to the project. 

**Xinjiang Xinhui hopes to upgrade its small smelter** Elsewhere in China, Xinjiang Xinhui Copper Company, a holding company for Zhaojin Mining Industry Company, is looking to expand its small existing smelter in the Kashgar, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.  At present, the company operates a 10kt/a blister copper plant and aims to raise this to between 90-100kt/a in two stages.  It is thought that while EIA approval is not likely to be a major issue in this remote region, the bottleneck to the company’s objective of commissioning the project before 2013 is likely to be the general lack of infrastructure. 

**Potential new refinery in Jiangxi province to treat 3**<sup>**rd**</sup> **party blister** The third project identified this month is Zhejiang Zhiyuan Co’s 100kt/a refinery project in Raoyushan Industrial Park, Jiangxi Province.  The project, which is expected to cost $200M and take one year to build, will employ 200 people and will source blister from scrap smel

ters in the region. 

**Tanzania to get its first copper smelter?** Outside China came the announcement from Dubai-based City Energy & Infrastructure LLC that it plans to build east Africa’s first copper smelter (along with a sugar plant) in Tanzania over the next three years with a total investment of $500M.  Given that the capacity of the project is expected to be 300kt/a, we are somewhat surprised at the very modest anticipated investment requirement.  Even in China the likely capex would be close to $1bn for a modern compliant plant of this scale and we would expect a figure of closer to $1.5Bn for such a project outside China.  As regards feed supply, Tanzania produces only 50kt/a of concentrates as a by-product from gold mining and hence the majority of the project’s feed requirements would need to be satisfied via the international market. In a similar vein, cathode demand in North Africa and the Middle East is satisfied by existing producers in Zambia, the DRC, Iran etc. and hence there is no pressing requirement to have another supplier to this regional market at present. 

**Mating Season progress rather slow thus far** Progress in the annual Mating Season negotiations has been rather slow over the past month.  With many buyers and sellers now well into their first round discussions we have yet to hear of numbers being tabled by any of the parties involved.  BHP Billiton is thought to be continuing with its strategy of exploring and developing alternative mechanisms for establishing TC/RCs.  The company is seemingly keen on establishing a three-pronged settlement that considers a combination of an annual TC/RC, a shorter-term (six month) number and also a percentage based on spot market terms, as opposed to a plain vanilla annual benchmark. Elsewhere, uncertainties loom large in the Freeport camp, with the company having declared force majeure at its Indonesian mine and with the spectre of possible production disruptions down the line at its Peruvian joint-venture which is also subject to ongoing industrial action.  Because of these factors, the company is unlikely to be best placed this year to take the lead in establishing a benchmark.  And so with the two usual candidates looking increasingly unlikely at leading the way forward in the standard Mating Season negotiations, the question then begs as to who else might be in a position to assume this role.  One of the main issues for some of the other concentrate sellers is that they are too small to qualify for major seller status while for others, their contracts stipulate that settlements must reference other deals between major buyers and sellers, thereby precluding them from establishing a benchmark.  Ultimately a market reference will be established one way or another, but under these current circumstances, the numbers are likely to be far closer to last year’s Mating Season settlement than to current spot rates.

## Production news 

**Strike action takes 100kt copper out of circulation this year** Barely a day has gone by over the past two months that strike action at various copper mines somewhere has not been mentioned.  In all, we estimate that in excess of 100kt copper production has been lost during the first nine months of this year through the issue of deteriorating labour relations alone.  The one positive ray of light came from Zambia late this month, where strike action at both of the Chinese-owned Chambishi copper operations (mine and smelter) came to a close after starting on October 4

<sup>th</sup> .  The nature of the agreements between the labour unions and owners is not yet clear, and neither is the amount of lost production.  That said the mine produces 25kt/a of copper-in-concentrates andd8kt/a of SxEw copper while the smelter output is much higher at 170kt/a using third party feed. 

Elsewhere, a new issue surfaced in Finland, with Metalworkers Unions (comprising Nordic IN, EMF and IMF) and the salaried employees unions (Pro and the Federation of Professional and Managerial Staff YTN) going on strike on October 21<sup>st</sup> following a breakdown in negotiations with the government.  Boliden promptly closed its Harjavalta copper smelter and Kokkola zinc smelter, and acknowledged that the strike action might have continued through to November 7<sup>th</sup> .  However, by the 25<sup>th</sup> the Metalworkers Unions and Pro had accepted the proposal put forward by the State mediator, and a new collective agreement is now in place running to the end of October 2013.  Unfortunately, as of the 27<sup>th</sup> the YTN union had not renewed the agreement, and so a strike of professional and managerial staff still threatens the industry.  This has not prevented Boliden from re-starting its Finnish smelters, though, and they were fired back up over the course of the 24-25<sup>th</sup> of the month. 

**Strikes take 32kt copper off Freeport’s bottom line in Q3…** Despite the cumulative loss of mine output of 23 days at Grasberg (8 in July, and on-off activity since September 15<sup>th</sup> ) and on-off strike action for virtually the month of September in Peru, the company announced in its Q3 report that the impact to the end of last month in terms of lost metal had been contained to c.31.8kt copper and 100k ozs gold.  This is because virtually all of this has come from Grasberg alone, as a combination of salaried staff, maintenance crews and non-striking workers at Cerro Verde has left output from this operation pretty well unscathed so far. 

**..FM declared at Grasberg** Meanwhile, the situation at Grasberg remains unpredictable – as it has done for much of the month – with the better days seeing more workers return to their posts, and the worst days seeing the untimely demise of individuals as a result of gun fire.  By September 26<sup>th</sup> , though, Freeport considered the situation to be serious enough to declare force majeure on concentrate shipments, with actual production having been halted indefinitely a couple of days prior. 

The pipeline is arguably the most vulnerable point in the Grasberg supply chain.  There are three pipes taking concentrate down from the mill to the port and two pipes taking diesel up, and although a series of valves allows repairs to be made within hours, there had been three incidents this month alone when the pipes were cut.  At times, the mine and mill has managed to maintain a 50% operating rate, but continued action through to mid-November has been promised by the unions, prompting d

aily reconsideration by Freeport as to the validity of continued operations at all while the disruption persists.

**Codelco likely to buy into Anglo American Sur - with help from Mitsui…** Chilean parastatal miner Codelco has ensured that it will be in a position to exercise its option to buy up to 49% of the shares in Anglo American Sur by accepting Mitsui & Co.’s offer of up to US$6.75B of debt financing.  The company has the right to exercise the option in the month of January every three years through to 2027; with January 2012 being the next “open window” period, the timing of this financial arrangement with Mitsui & Co brings speculation that Codelco intends to act at this first available opportunity.  A second agreement with Mitsui & Co allows Codelco to settle a portion of the loan with an indirect 50% stake in any shareholding in Anglo Sur acquired by Codelco, based on a pre-determined value of the 49% interest of c.US$9.76B.  Anglo Sur’s producing assets include the Los Bronces mine, which produced c.217kt copper in concentrate and SxEw cathode last year, El Soldado (40kt) and the C

hagres smelter (138kt).  These assets go back to the time of oil producer Exxon and local partner Cia Disputada de las Condes.  The option to buy this minority stake was originally granted to Enami but was transferred to Codelco in 2008.  The agreement does not cover the assets known as Anglo American Norte, which include the wholly-owned Mantos Blancos and Mantoverde or Anglo’s 44% interest in Collahuasi. Anglo is in the throes of commissioning a US$2.5B expansion at Los Bronces which should see concentrate output increase to between 425-450kt/a during the 2012-2014 period, and level out at 350kt/a from 2015. 

**..and gives green light to u/g expansion at Chuqui** Codelco has also given the go ahead to spend US$875M on early works for an expansion at Chuquicamata.  The existing 430kt/a open pit mine is expected to enter its final production stages by 2017, and be reduced to a sub-100kt/a producer by 2020.  This new expenditure should convert operations to underground and maintain production at between 300-400kt/a from 2018-2019, and is likely to cost c.US$2B in total. Underground reserves are put at 1.7Bt of 0.7% Cu and could extend mine life by 50 years.  Codelco’s moves on Anglo American Sur and the expansion at Chuqui came shortly after its September announcement of an expansion at the San Antonio deposit of the Salvador division, which would cost c.US$330M and see output at Salvador maintained at 7580kt/a through to the end of this decade. 

**Metallum Holdings places orders for new equipment at Beerse** Metallum Holdings SA continues to upgrade its Beerse-based Metallo secondary smelter/refinery complex in Belgium.  Earlier this year, Andritz Metals received an order for a 220-t gas-fired Maerz drum furnace.  This should allow higher volumes of copper scrap to be melted as well as free up bottlenecks at the existing top blown rotary converters.  This has now been followed up by a late-September order to SMS Meer for a new 50-tph anode casting wheel, which will complement the existing 20-year old unit and allow a more efficient production split of “clean” copper anodes and highly impure copper anodes.  SMS Meer believes the new wheel should increase mould service life by up to 20%, reduce plant costs and increase productivity. 

Beerse currently has a 105kt/a secondary smelter and a 25kt/a refinery producing clean and impure anodes.  Metallo recovers significant amounts of tin, nickel, lead and precious metals via other selective process equipment, and is the single European tin producer of LME branded low lead tin.  The new equipment should allow higher sales (up to 150kt/a) of clean anodes (and thus higher revenues) to third parties, and optimised in-house processing of impure anodes (between 35-40kt/a).  The revisions to the process route brought about by the new equipment, which should all be commissioned by Q3 2012, will increase recoverable quantities of nickel products.

**BHPB lays out its grand plans for Olympic Dam** Early this month, and following the receipt of local and national environmental approvals, BHP Billiton gave the go-ahead for US$1.2B in pre-commitment capital for a possible four-fold expansion of its Olympic Dam copper-uranium nine in South Australia.  The capex will go towards long-lead items such as site infrastructure development, trucks and accommodation, but most of it is conditional on the success of certain political agreements through the local parliament.  The current 180kt/a copper producer could go to 750kt/a and remain open pit in a staged expansion, with the first step to 350kt/a being targeted for 2017.  Output this past quarter was down to c.40kt refined metal due to a planned maintenance at the smelter and refinery.  Meanwhile, expansion progress at the company’s part-owned Antamina property in Peru is well under way, and this US$435M expenditure should see the mine increase output from the current operating rate of c.350kt/a to 440kt/a by the end of this year.  Payable copper was already up to 30.3kt in Q3 this year, from 23.2kt a year ago, assisted by higher milling rates and head grades.  Finally, the dramatic decline in Q3 output at its 57.5%-held Escondida in Chile was highlighted in the report, down to c.50kt payable copper (attributable) from 111kt a year ago.  Lower head grades (0.97% Cu _vs._ 1.24% Cu) and industrial action in July/August were largely responsible for the drop. 

**Boliden mine output down, but metal output surges** Swedish miner Boliden saw its lowest copper in concentrate production level this past quarter of just under 20kt since Q1 2010’s 13.6kt, but record refined copper output of 90kt vs. 76.5kt in Q2 and 82.4kt for Q3 2010.  In common with many other mines across the world, Boliden’s leading copper mine asset – Aitik in Sweden – saw mining pass through lean ore grade areas during this past quarter, forcing the drop in output from 17.5kt in Q2 this year to 16.9kt in Q3.  This is likely to leave Aitik’s output for this year somewhat closer to 2010’s 67.2kt copper in concentrates than we originally thought.  Smelter and refinery production for the group remained quite firm, however.  Smelter throughput and refined cathode at Ronnskar dropped only by 1% to 202.4kt and 55.4kt, respectively, while concentrates smelted at Harjavalta increased by a significant 37% during Q3 this year vs. the same period in 2010 to 133kt, with refined cathode increasing similarly (+31%) to 34.7kt.  A higher equipment availability rate during the period was largely responsible for the increase.
